# Draft:List of major cities in the United States lacking intra-urban rail transit

Although many American cities feature some form of intra-urban rail in their public transit systems, many major cities and regional population centers in the United States are not connected by rail-based transit systems.
History
The first rail-based rapid transit system in the United States was the New York Subway, with the IRT Ninth Avenue Line opening as an elevated railway in 1868. Many other cities soon followed suit, with (in chronological order) Chicago, Boston, Philadelphia, northern New Jersey, and Cleveland constructing new rapid transit systems between the 1890s and the 1950s, with Cincinnati starting on a subway system but abandoning it during construction in the wake of the stock market crash of 1929. Another subway boom began in the 1970s due to the establishment of the Urban Mass Transit Administration opening new avenues for federal funding, spurring the development of new rapid transit systems in San Francisco and Oakland, Washington DC, Atlanta, Baltimore, Miami, and Los Angeles. However, rising costs and urban decay have led to lessening interest in the development of rapid transit systems. Light rail, a form of rail transit that operates on a mix of exclusive rights of way and along surface streets, surged in the 1970s and 1980s as it began to be seen as an intermediate option for cities who did not want to invest as much money into full rapid transit systems. Many mid-sized American cities such as Portland, San Diego, Seattle, Dallas, Houston, Newark, Salt Lake City, and Minneapolis began to opt for light rail over heavy rail due to cost savings, with other larger cities such as Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Boston opted to integrate light rail as a part of their rapid transit systems.
Streetcars, conversely, have long been popular in American cities due to their growth historically outpacing the speed at which roads could be paved, disallowing the horsebuses that were used in European cities and instead creating a niche for horse-drawn trams. These lines were later electrified to save on operating costs, and although many were torn out in favor of car-centric development, a handful were kept, including well-known lines in New Orleans and San Francisco. Modern streetcars began to come back into favor with the development of a new streetcar line along an old route in Portland, Oregon in 2001, seen as ways to revitalize inner-city neighborhoods at a lower cost than rapid transit systems or light rail. They differ from the other systems by being almost entirely street running and having level boarding. Many cities have reused or repurposed old streetcar routes for their modern streetcar or light rail systems.
The smallest city in the United States to have intra-urban rail rapid transit is likely Morgantown, West Virginia. With a population of just over 30,000, it has a small people mover system on the campus of West Virginia University.
Cities lacking intra-urban rail transit
The following cities lack any sort of rail transit in their respective metropolitan areas, including but not limited to commuter rail, subways or metros, light rail, streetcars, monorails, or people movers.
